items.q: If you stand near a radioactive source, do you become radioactive?
items.correct: No — being irradiated (exposed) does not make you radioactive; only contamination with radioactive material does.
items.misconception: Yes, standing near a source makes you radioactive too.
items.why: Irradiation is exposure to the rays. It doesn't add radioactive atoms. Contamination — radioactive material getting on or inside you — is what makes something radioactive.

items.q: Which type of radiation is the most strongly ionising?
items.correct: Alpha — it is the most ionising but the least penetrating (stopped by paper).
items.misconception: Gamma, because it is the most penetrating and dangerous.
items.why: Alpha is large with a +2 charge, so it ionises strongly but is absorbed quickly. Gamma penetrates far but ionises weakly — penetration and ionising power trade off.

items.correct: It is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air and can't get through skin from outside.
items.misconception: Alpha is the most penetrating and passes straight through the body.
items.why: Alpha particles are large and highly charged, so they're absorbed almost at once. They're mainly a hazard if the source is inhaled or swallowed.
